source.title: End-to-End Training for Unified Tokenization and Latent Denoising
source.authors: Shivam Duggal; Xingjian Bai; Zongze Wu; Richard Zhang; Eli Shechtman; Antonio Torralba; Phillip Isola; William T. Freeman

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figures and tables are flattened in the web text.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports representational alignment between tokenization and denoising pathways, but does not test convergence between independently trained models or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The reported CKA/CKNNA and cosine results concern activations from tokenization and denoising pathways in the study’s training setup. They do not measure similarity of distances across independently trained models, cross-modal alignment, or convergence with scale. These pathway-alignment findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The CKA/CKNNA and cosine results compare the tokenization and denoising pathways of one jointly trained system. The denoiser is supervised to predict the encoder's latent, so their alignment is built in by the training target. Even the separate encoder–denoiser ablation is coupled this way, so it is not a pair of independently trained models. No cross-model, cross-modal, cross-seed, scale or metric-dependence test of convergence is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors add that the shared model separates the two modes mainly through normalization and scale parameters, supported by an entropy analysis, while attention and MLP computation is reused. They note that CKA is largely insensitive to norm/scale changes, so the pathways differ more in calibration than in geometry.
record.recipe_differences: Measures within-model pathway activation alignment with CKA/CKNNA and cosine similarity; it does not apply a cross-model convergence method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported pathway alignment is lower when denoising gradients are allowed to backpropagate through the clean latent rather than using stop-gradient.

fits_no_version.finding: With stop-gradient, both the weight-shared encoder and the separate encoder–denoiser show high tokenization–denoising CKA/CKNNA alignment, especially in later layers (figure only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jointly trained tokenization and denoising pathways that share a latent target develop similar internal activations, even in separate networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Letting denoising gradients flow through the clean latent reduces late-layer CKA alignment in both settings. Final-latent cosine similarity also drops at lower timesteps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backpropagating denoising gradients through clean latents weakens tokenization–denoising pathway alignment.

record.problems: The alignment results are presented in figures without numerical values or reported uncertainty. The measured alignment is between pathways in a jointly trained system, not between independently trained models.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure representational alignment relevant to the claim. Reconstruction, generation, and compression metrics were not included because they do not measure the claim’s representation-alignment outcomes.

untested.parts: No comparison of independently trained models across scale, architecture, objective or data.
No vision–language alignment on paired images and captions.
No same-architecture networks from different seeds.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation transfer between distinct models.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
CKA, CKNNA and cosine are used, but their dependence on settings or inputs is not tested for cross-model convergence.
Does not test whether cross-model convergence is incomplete, plateaus, or is explained by shared data or objectives.

record.verdict_notes: Phillip Isola, an author of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, is a co-author, and the paper uses the CKNNA metric. However, it neither cites nor tests the hypothesis. All rows correctly have versions ['none']. Alignment values are figure-only, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data as they scale.
Does not measure alignment between vision and language models on paired images and captions.
Does not compare same-architecture networks trained from different initializations for shared features or subspaces.
Does not test mapping or interchangeability between distinct models’ representations, layer stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mapping.
Does not compare recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Although it reports CKA/CKNNA and cosine similarity, it does not test metric, input, or distribution dependence of cross-model convergence.
Does not test whether cross-model convergence is incomplete or explained by shared training data or objectives.

rows.subject: UNITE (weight-shared Generative Encoder)
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment between tokenization-pathway and denoising-pathway activations using CKA/CKNNA.
rows.measure: Representational alignment across layers; authors describe it as high, especially in later layers.
rows.note: The text describes strong alignment. This is within-model pathway alignment, not cross-model convergence.

rows.subject: separate encoder–denoiser ablation
rows.operation_detail: Measured alignment between encoder/tokenization-pathway and denoising-pathway activations using CKA/CKNNA.
rows.measure: Representational alignment across layers; authors describe it as high, especially in later layers.
rows.note: The text describes strong alignment despite separate encoder and denoiser networks; this is not a comparison of independently trained models.

rows.subject: UNITE (weight-shared Generative Encoder)
rows.operation_detail: Measured CKA/CKNNA alignment between tokenization and denoising activations with denoising gradients backpropagated through the clean latent.
rows.measure: Representational alignment across layers; authors report reduced alignment relative to the stop-gradient variant, including weaker late-layer alignment.
rows.note: The text says alignment is reduced, not absent.
